items.title: Sustainable Carbon Use
items.summary: Sustainable solutions for current global challenges, such as the carbon budget, circular…
items.content_html: Sustainable solutions for current global challenges, such as the carbon budget, circular economy, human health, and clean energy, through synthetic biology. My research program will focus on developing microbes as green cell factories with tailor-made catalysts that can convert biomass-derived feedstocks into fuels, valuable commodities, or pharmaceutical products. This research is centered around two short- term goals: 1) Developing designer catalysts via enzyme evolution to enhance the metabolic process and create new carbon sinks, and 2) Engineering green factories with designer catalysts that can simultaneously degrade lignocellulosic waste and produce valuable commodities. Over the next five years, my research program will prioritize the development of energy-efficient enzymes and improvements in metabolic engineering efforts to convert available biomass into valuable commodities, paving the way for sustainable chemistry.

items.title: Metabolic Engineering for Waste Valorization
items.summary: The Joshi Lab waste valorization project is an interwoven research cycle with…
items.content_html: The Joshi Lab waste valorization project is an interwoven research cycle with the goal of producing new to nature industrially viable enzymes capable of degrading a variety of waste and contributing to microbial upcycling. We begin with in-silico candidate generation followed by directed evolution methods to probe the sequence/fitness landscape of these candidates and improve their viability. Industry-ready enzymes will be used for degradation of various recalcitrant polymers (e.g., plastic and lignocellulose) into more bio-accessible small molecules. These molecules, along with the enzymes themselves, are essential inputs for both existing and novel microbial upcycling systems that produce biomass, bioenergy or value-added chemicals invaluable to a variety of industries. As we make exciting developments in these three connected processes, the data we produce will be back-channeled to our machine learning model: training it in generating novel enzyme sequences, narrowing down candidates and making sequence-structure-function inferences for rational design modifications to make our enzymes as effective as possible.
